Ordinary Differential Equations

Calculation Arena & Practice
Question Set
Qty: / 10
  • $F(t, y, y', \dots, y^{(n)}) = 0$
    • Order
      • 1st Order: $y' = f(t,y)$
      • 2nd Order: $y'' = f(t,y,y')$
    • Linearity
      • Linear: $a_n(t)y^{(n)} + \dots = g(t)$
      • Non-Linear: $y^2, \sin(y), yy'$
    • Autonomy
      • Autonomous: $F(y,y',\dots)=0$
      • Non-Autonomous: $t$ appears explicitly
    • Equilibrium Solutions
      • $y'=F(t,y)$, set $F(t,\bar{y})=0$
  • Solve $y' = f(t,y)$
    • Separable?
      • $\int M dt + \int N dy = C$
    • Linear?
      • $\mu = e^{\int p dt}, y = \frac{1}{\mu}\int \mu q$
    • Exact?
      • $\Psi_t=M, \Psi_y=N$
  • Transformations
    • Bernoulli: $y' + p(t)y = q(t)y^n$
      • Sub $v = y^{1-n}$
    • Homogeneous: $y' = F(y/t)$
      • Sub $v = y/t \Rightarrow y=tv$
    • Exact + Integrating Factor
      • $\mu(t)$ if $\frac{M_y - N_t}{N} = g(t)$
      • $\mu(y)$ if $\frac{N_t - M_y}{M} = h(y)$
      • $\mu(ty)$ if $\frac{N_t - M_y}{tM - yN} = L(ty)$ (advanced)
  • $y'' + p(t)y' + q(t)y = g(t)$
    • Reduce to 1st Order
      • $y''=F(t,y')$: sub $p=y'$
    • Constant Coeff: $ay''+by'+cy=0$
      • Characteristic Eq: $ar^2+br+c=0$
        • $\Delta>0$: $y=c_1 e^{r_1 t}+c_2 e^{r_2 t}$
        • $\Delta<0$: $y=e^{\alpha t}(c_1\cos\beta t+c_2\sin\beta t)$
        • $\Delta=0$: $y=(c_1+c_2 t)e^{rt}$
    • Wronskian & Superposition
      • $W(y_1,y_2)=y_1 y_2'-y_1' y_2$
      • Reduction of Order
    • Euler Equation: $t^2 y''+\alpha t y'+\beta y=0$
      • Sub $y=t^r \Rightarrow$ indicial eq
  • Existence & Uniqueness
    • 1st Order Linear (Thm 4.1)
      • $p,q$ continuous on $(\alpha,\beta)$ → global unique sol
    • 1st Order Non-Linear (Thm 4.2)
      • $f, f_y$ continuous on $R$ → local unique sol
      • Non-uniqueness: $y'=y^{1/3}$
      • Blow-up: $y'=y^2$
    • Peano (Thm 4.8): $f$ continuous → existence only
    • Picard Iteration
      • $\phi_{n+1}=y_0+\int_{t_0}^{t}f(s,\phi_n)ds$
    • 2nd Order Linear E&U
      • $p,q,g$ continuous → global unique sol

Theorems & Proofs

Thm 4.1
1. Linear Existence & Uniqueness Theorem
Theorem (Thm 4.1): Suppose $p(t)$ and $q(t)$ are continuous on $(\alpha, \beta)$. Then for any $t_0 \in (\alpha, \beta)$, $y_0 \in \mathbb{R}$, there exists a unique solution to $y' = p(t)y + q(t)$, $y(t_0)=y_0$ defined on the entire interval $(\alpha, \beta)$.

Proof (Existence): Define the integrating factor $$\mu(t) = \exp\!\left(-\int_{t_0}^t p(s)\,ds\right), \quad \mu(t_0)=1.$$ Since $p$ is continuous on $(\alpha,\beta)$, $\mu(t)$ is continuous and nonzero there. The general solution formula $$y(t) = \frac{1}{\mu(t)}\left(\int_{t_0}^t \mu(s)q(s)\,ds + c\right)$$ is well-defined for all $t\in(\alpha,\beta)$, establishing existence.

Proof (Uniqueness): Applying the initial condition $y(t_0)=y_0$ forces $c = y_0$, giving the unique particular solution $$y(t) = \frac{1}{\mu(t)}\left(\int_{t_0}^t \mu(s)q(s)\,ds + y_0\right).$$ Since $c$ is uniquely determined, the solution is unique on all of $(\alpha,\beta)$.

Key point: Unlike the nonlinear case, the solution exists globally on the entire interval where $p$ and $q$ are continuous.
Thm 4.2
2. Non-Linear Existence & Uniqueness Theorem
Theorem (Thm 4.2 — Picard–Lindelöf): Let $R = \{(t,y):|t-t_0|\le a,\,|y-y_0|\le b\}$. If $f(t,y)$ and $\tfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ are continuous on $R$, then the IVP $y'=f(t,y),\,y(t_0)=y_0$ has a unique solution on $[t_0-h,\,t_0+h]$, where $h=\min\!\left(a,\,\tfrac{b}{M}\right)$ and $M=\max_{R}|f|$.

Proof sketch (Picard iteration, 4 steps):
The IVP is equivalent to the integral equation $y(t)=y_0+\int_{t_0}^t f(s,y(s))\,ds$. Define iterates $\phi_0(t)=y_0$ and $$\phi_{n+1}(t)=y_0+\int_{t_0}^t f(s,\phi_n(s))\,ds.$$ Step 1 (Iterates stay in $R$): By induction, $|\phi_n(t)-y_0|\le M|t-t_0|\le Mh\le b$ for all $t\in[t_0-h,t_0+h]$, so $(t,\phi_n(t))\in R$.

Step 2 (Uniform convergence): Since $\tfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ is continuous on the compact set $R$, there exists $K>0$ with $|f(t,y_1)-f(t,y_2)|\le K|y_1-y_2|$ (Lipschitz condition). By induction, $$|\phi_{n}(t)-\phi_{n-1}(t)|\le \frac{MK^{n-1}|t-t_0|^n}{n!}\le \frac{MK^{n-1}h^n}{n!}.$$ The series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{MK^{n-1}h^n}{n!}=\frac{M}{K}(e^{Kh}-1)$ converges, so by the Weierstrass M-test $\{\phi_n\}$ converges uniformly to some $\phi$ on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$.

Step 3 (Limit is a solution): By uniform convergence and continuity of $f$, $$\phi(t)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\phi_{n+1}(t)=y_0+\int_{t_0}^t f(s,\phi(s))\,ds,$$ so $\phi$ satisfies the integral equation, hence the IVP.

Step 4 (Uniqueness): If $\phi$ and $\omega$ both solve the integral equation, let $g(t)=\int_{t_0}^t|\phi-\omega|\,ds$. Then $g'\le Kg$, $g(t_0)=0$. Multiplying by $e^{-Kt}$ gives $(e^{-Kt}g)'\le 0$, so $g(t)\le 0$, hence $\phi=\omega$. $\blacksquare$

Note: Guarantees only local existence (on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$, not necessarily all of $\mathbb{R}$). Blow-up is possible even when $f,f_y$ are globally continuous (e.g.\ $y'=y^2$, $y(0)=1$ blows up at $t=1$).
Thm 4.8
3. Peano Existence Theorem
Theorem (Thm 4.8 — Peano): If $f(t,y)$ is continuous on $R = \{(t,y):|t-t_0|\le a,\,|y-y_0|\le b\}$, then the IVP $y'=f(t,y),\,y(t_0)=y_0$ has at least one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ where $h=\min(a,b/M)$ and $M=\max_R|f|$.

Proof idea: The proof uses the Picard iterates $\phi_{n+1}(t)=y_0+\int_{t_0}^t f(s,\phi_n(s))\,ds$ together with the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem: the iterates form an equicontinuous, uniformly bounded family, so a uniformly convergent subsequence exists. Its limit satisfies the integral equation. (Full proof requires real analysis and is omitted in this course.)

Key contrast with Thm 4.2:
  • Peano (continuity of $f$ only) → existence, but not uniqueness.
  • Picard–Lindelöf (continuity of $f$ and $f_y$) → existence and uniqueness.
Example: $y'=y^{1/3}$, $y(0)=0$. Here $f_y=\tfrac{1}{3}y^{-2/3}$ is undefined at $y=0$, so Thm 4.2 fails. Peano guarantees at least one solution; in fact infinitely many exist: $y\equiv 0$ and $y=\left(\tfrac{2}{3}(t-t^*)\right)^{3/2}$ for any $t^*\ge 0$.
Thm 5.1
4. Second-Order Linear Existence & Uniqueness
Theorem (Thm 5.1): Consider the IVP $y'' + p(t)y' + q(t)y = g(t)$, $y(t_0)=y_0$, $y'(t_0)=y_1$. If $p(t)$, $q(t)$, and $g(t)$ are continuous on an open interval $I$ containing $t_0$, then there exists a unique solution $y(t)$ defined on the entire interval $I$.

Proof idea: The proof parallels the Picard iteration for first-order systems. Rewrite as a first-order system $\mathbf{u}'=\mathbf{F}(t,\mathbf{u})$ with $\mathbf{u}=(y,y')^T$. Since $p,q,g$ are continuous on $I$, the vector field $\mathbf{F}$ is continuous and Lipschitz in $\mathbf{u}$ on any compact sub-interval. Picard iteration then yields a unique local solution, and linearity of the ODE allows extension to all of $I$ (no blow-up is possible for linear equations). Full details use the same uniform-convergence argument as Thm 4.2 and are omitted in this course.

Key contrasts:
  • vs.\ 1st-order linear (Thm 4.1): same global conclusion, now requires two initial conditions.
  • vs.\ 1st-order nonlinear (Thm 4.2): linear 2nd-order is still global; nonlinear may only be local.
Example: $y'' + \frac{e^t}{t^2-3t}y' - \frac{\sin(t+3)}{t^2-3t}y = 0$, $y(1)=2$, $y'(1)=1$. Coefficients are discontinuous at $t=0$ and $t=3$; the largest interval containing $t_0=1$ where they are continuous is $(0,3)$, so a unique solution exists on $(0,3)$.
Thm 5.2
5. Principle of Superposition
Theorem (Thm 5.5 — Superposition): If $y_1$ and $y_2$ are solutions of $L[y]:=a(t)y''+b(t)y'+c(t)y=0$, then for any constants $c_1,c_2\in\mathbb{R}$, the function $y=c_1y_1+c_2y_2$ is also a solution.

Proof: Since $L$ is a linear operator, $$L[c_1y_1+c_2y_2]=c_1L[y_1]+c_2L[y_2]=c_1\cdot 0+c_2\cdot 0=0. \quad\blacksquare$$ Consequence: From two solutions we can construct an infinite family $S=\{c_1y_1+c_2y_2\mid c_1,c_2\in\mathbb{R}\}$. Whether this family contains all solutions depends on the Wronskian (see Thm 5.8).

This does not hold for nonlinear ODEs. For example, $y'=y^2$ has solutions $y=\frac{1}{1-t}$ and $y=0$, but their sum is not a solution.
Thm 5.3
6. Abel's Theorem (Wronskian)
Theorem (Thm 5.10 — Abel's Theorem): Let $p,q$ be continuous on an open interval $I$. If $y_1,y_2$ are solutions of $y''+p(t)y'+q(t)y=0$, then $$W(y_1,y_2)(t)=c\exp\!\left(-\int p(t)\,dt\right)$$ for some constant $c$ depending on $y_1,y_2$ but not on $t$. Consequently $W$ is either always zero or never zero on $I$.

Proof: Differentiate the Wronskian $W=y_1y_2'-y_2y_1'$: $$W'=y_1y_2''-y_2y_1''.$$ Since $y_1,y_2$ satisfy the ODE: $y_i''=-p(t)y_i'-q(t)y_i$. Substituting, $$W'=y_1(-py_2'-qy_2)-y_2(-py_1'-qy_1)=-p(y_1y_2'-y_2y_1')=-p(t)W.$$ This is a first-order linear ODE for $W$. Solving by integrating factors: $$W(t)=W(t_0)\exp\!\left(-\int_{t_0}^t p(s)\,ds\right). \quad\blacksquare$$ Corollary: If $W(t_0)\ne 0$ for some $t_0\in I$, then $W(t) e 0$ for all $t\in I$, and $\{y_1,y_2\}$ form a fundamental set of solutions (FSS); the general solution is $y=c_1y_1+c_2y_2$.
Thm 3.4
7. Exactness Test
Theorem (Thm 3.4 — Exactness Test): Suppose $M,N,M_y,N_t$ are continuous on a rectangle $R=(\alpha,\beta) \times(\gamma,\delta)$. Then $$M(t,y)+N(t,y)y'=0 \text{ is exact} \iff M_y(t,y)=N_t(t,y) \text{ for all }(t,y)\in R.$$ Proof ($\Rightarrow$): If exact, $\exists\,\Psi$ with $\Psi_t=M$, $\Psi_y=N$. By symmetry of mixed partials, $M_y=\Psi_{ty}=\Psi_{yt}=N_t$.

Proof ($\Leftarrow$): Assume $M_y=N_t$. Construct $\Psi$ by integrating $\Psi_t=M$ with respect to $t$: $$\Psi(t,y)=\int_{t_0}^t M(s,y)\,ds+h(y).$$ Differentiating with respect to $y$ and requiring $\Psi_y=N$: $$h'(y)=N(t,y)-\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\int_{t_0}^t M(s,y)\,ds.$$ The RHS is independent of $t$ (verified by differentiating w.r.t.\ $t$ and using $M_y=N_t$), so $h(y)$ is well-defined. Hence $\Psi$ exists and the ODE is exact. $\blacksquare$

Solution method: Once $\Psi$ is found, the general (implicit) solution is $\Psi(t,y)=C$. For IVP $y(t_0)=y_0$: $\Psi(t,y)=\Psi(t_0,y_0)$.
Thm 5.8
8. Fundamental Set of Solutions (FSS) Criterion
Theorem (Thm 5.8): Let $p,q$ be continuous on $I$, and let $y_1,y_2$ be solutions of $y''+p(t)y'+q(t)y=0$. Then any solution $y$ can be written as $y=c_1y_1+c_2y_2$ $\iff$ $\exists\,t_0\in I$ such that $W(y_1,y_2)(t_0)\ne 0$.

Proof ($\Leftarrow$): Let $\phi$ be any solution. Since $W(t_0)\ne 0$, the linear system $$\begin{pmatrix}y_1(t_0)&y_2(t_0)\\y_1'(t_0)&y_2'(t_0)\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}c_1\\c_2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\phi(t_0)\\\phi'(t_0)\end{pmatrix}$$ has a unique solution $(c_1^*,c_2^*)$. Then $z=c_1^*y_1+c_2^*y_2$ solves the same IVP as $\phi$. By uniqueness (Thm 5.1), $\phi=z$. $\blacksquare$

Proof ($\Rightarrow$, contrapositive): If $W(t_0)=0$ for all $t_0\in I$, the linear system above has no solution for some $(x_0,x_1)$. The IVP with those initial conditions has a solution $\psi$ (by Thm 5.1) that cannot be written as $c_1y_1+c_2y_2$. $\blacksquare$

When $W\ne 0$, we call $(y_1,y_2)$ a fundamental set of solutions (FSS). By Abel's theorem, $W\ne 0$ at one point implies $W\ne 0$ everywhere on $I$.
Thm 5.12
9. Existence of Fundamental Set of Solutions
Theorem (Thm 5.12): Let $p,q$ be continuous on $I$ and $t_0\in I$. Let $y_1$ solve the IVP with $y(t_0)=1,\,y'(t_0)=0$, and $y_2$ solve the IVP with $y(t_0)=0,\,y'(t_0)=1$. Then $(y_1,y_2)$ is a FSS.

Proof: Both $y_1,y_2$ exist by Thm 5.1. Compute the Wronskian at $t_0$: $$W(y_1,y_2)(t_0)=\begin{vmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{vmatrix}=1\ne 0.$$ By Thm 5.8, $(y_1,y_2)$ is a FSS. $\blacksquare$

Note: The FSS is not unique — any two linearly independent solutions form a FSS. For example, $y''-y=0$ has FSS $\{e^t,e^{-t}\}$ and also $\{\cosh t,\sinh t\}$.
Thm 6.4
10. Real & Imaginary Parts of Complex Solution
Theorem (Thm 6.4): If $y(t)=u(t)+iv(t)$ is a complex-valued solution of $y''+p(t)y'+q(t)y=0$ with real-valued $p,q$, then both $u(t)$ and $v(t)$ are real solutions.

Proof: Substituting into the ODE: $$0=(u''+iv'')+(p(t))(u'+iv')+(q(t))(u+iv)=(u''+pu'+qu)+i(v''+pv'+qv).$$ A complex number is zero iff both real and imaginary parts are zero, so $u''+pu'+qu=0$ and $v''+pv'+qv=0$. $\blacksquare$

Application (complex roots $\Delta<0$): Characteristic roots $r_{1,2}=\lambda\pm i\mu$ give complex solution $e^{(\lambda+i\mu)t}=e^{\lambda t}(\cos\mu t+i\sin\mu t)$. By this theorem, the real-valued FSS is: $$y_1=e^{\lambda t}\cos\mu t,\quad y_2=e^{\lambda t}\sin\mu t.$$ Their Wronskian is $W=\mu e^{2\lambda t}\ne 0$ (since $\mu\ne 0$), confirming they form a FSS.
Method
11. Reduction of Order
Method (Reduction of Order): Given one nonzero solution $y_1$ of $y''+p(t)y'+q(t)y=0$, find a second linearly independent solution $y_2=v(t)y_1(t)$.

Derivation: Substitute $y=vy_1$ into the ODE. Using $y'=v'y_1+vy_1'$ and $y''=v''y_1+2v'y_1'+vy_1''$: $$y_1v''+(2y_1'+p(t)y_1)v'=0.$$ Set $z=v'$ to get a first-order linear ODE: $$z'+\frac{2y_1'+p(t)y_1}{y_1}z=0.$$ Solving by separation: $$v'(t)=z(t)=\frac{1}{y_1^2(t)}\exp\!\left(-\int p(t)\,dt\right).$$ Integrating once more gives $v(t)$, and thus: $$y_2(t)=y_1(t)\int\frac{1}{y_1^2(t)}\,e^{-\int p(t)\,dt}\,dt.$$ Example (repeated root): For $ay''+by'+cy=0$ with $b^2=4ac$, $y_1=e^{-bt/(2a)}$. Reduction of order gives $y_2=te^{-bt/(2a)}$, confirming the general solution $y=(c_1+c_2t)e^{-bt/(2a)}$.
Method
12. Euler Equations
Euler Equation: $x^2y''+Axy'+By=0$, $x>0$, with constants $A,B$.

Method 1 — Substitution $t=\ln x$: Let $Y(t)=y(e^t)$. Then $xy'=Y'$ and $x^2y''=Y''-Y'$. The Euler equation becomes the constant-coefficient ODE: $$Y''+(A-1)Y'+BY=0.$$ Solve for $Y(t)$, then $y(x)=Y(\ln x)$.

Method 2 — Trial solution $y=x^r$: Substituting gives the indicial equation: $$r^2+(A-1)r+B=0.$$
  • Two distinct real roots $r_1\ne r_2$: $y=c_1x^{r_1}+c_2x^{r_2}$.
  • Repeated root $r_1=r_2=r$: $y=(c_1+c_2\ln x)x^r$.
  • Complex roots $\lambda\pm i\mu$: $y=x^\lambda(c_1\cos(\mu\ln x)+c_2\sin(\mu\ln x))$.
Example: $x^2y''+2xy'-6y=0$. Indicial equation: $r^2+r-6=(r+3)(r-2)=0$, so $r_1=-3,r_2=2$. General solution: $y=c_1x^{-3}+c_2x^2$.
Thm 8.1
13. Higher-Order Existence & Uniqueness
Theorem (Thm 8.1): Consider the IVP for an $n$th-order linear ODE: $$y^{(n)} + p_{n-1}(t)y^{(n-1)} + \cdots + p_1(t)y' + p_0(t)y = g(t)$$ with initial conditions $y(t_0)=y_0$, $y'(t_0)=y_1$, $\ldots$, $y^{(n-1)}(t_0)=y_{n-1}$.

If $p_0(t), p_1(t), \ldots, p_{n-1}(t)$ and $g(t)$ are continuous on an open interval $I$ containing $t_0$, then there exists a unique solution $y(t)$ defined on the entire interval $I$.

Proof idea: Convert to a first-order system of $n$ equations. Let $\mathbf{x} = (y, y', \ldots, y^{(n-1)})^T$. Then the ODE becomes $\mathbf{x}' = A(t)\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{g}(t)$ where $A(t)$ is the companion matrix. Since all coefficients are continuous on $I$, the vector field is continuous and Lipschitz. Picard iteration yields existence and uniqueness on $I$ (globally for linear equations).

Key point: For $n$th-order, we need exactly $n$ initial conditions: $y(t_0), y'(t_0), \ldots, y^{(n-1)}(t_0)$.
Thm 8.2
14. Superposition Principle (Higher-Order)
Theorem (Thm 8.2 — Superposition): If $y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n$ are solutions of the homogeneous $n$th-order linear ODE $$L[y] := y^{(n)} + p_{n-1}(t)y^{(n-1)} + \cdots + p_0(t)y = 0,$$ then for any constants $c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_n \in \mathbb{R}$, the function $$y = c_1y_1 + c_2y_2 + \cdots + c_ny_n$$ is also a solution.

Proof: Since $L$ is a linear operator (by definition, it involves only linear combinations of $y$ and its derivatives), $$L[c_1y_1 + \cdots + c_ny_n] = c_1L[y_1] + \cdots + c_nL[y_n] = c_1 \cdot 0 + \cdots + c_n \cdot 0 = 0. \quad\blacksquare$$
General Solution Structure: If $\{y_1, \ldots, y_n\}$ is a fundamental set (i.e., $W(y_1,\ldots,y_n) \neq 0$), then the general solution is $$y(t) = c_1y_1(t) + \cdots + c_ny_n(t) + y_p(t)$$ where $y_p$ is any particular solution to the non-homogeneous equation.
Thm 8.3
15. Abel's Theorem (Higher-Order Wronskian)
Theorem (Thm 8.3 — Abel's Theorem for $n$th-Order): Let $p_0, p_1, \ldots, p_{n-1}$ be continuous on an open interval $I$. If $y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n$ are solutions of $$y^{(n)} + p_{n-1}(t)y^{(n-1)} + \cdots + p_0(t)y = 0,$$ then their Wronskian satisfies $$W(y_1, \ldots, y_n)(t) = W(y_1, \ldots, y_n)(t_0) \exp\!\left(-\int_{t_0}^t p_{n-1}(s)\,ds\right)$$ for any $t_0 \in I$.

Proof sketch: The Wronskian $W(t)$ satisfies the first-order linear ODE $W' = -p_{n-1}(t)W$. This follows from differentiating the determinant definition of $W$ and using the fact that each $y_i$ satisfies the ODE. Solving this ODE gives the result.

Key consequence: $W(t) \neq 0$ at one point $t_0 \in I$ implies $W(t) \neq 0$ for all $t \in I$. Hence $\{y_1, \ldots, y_n\}$ is either always linearly independent or always linearly dependent on $I$.

Note: The coefficient $p_{n-1}(t)$ is the coefficient of $y^{(n-1)}$ in standard form (leading coefficient = 1).
Method
16. Characteristic Equation Method (Higher-Order)
Method: For constant-coefficient homogeneous ODE: $$a_ny^{(n)} + a_{n-1}y^{(n-1)} + \cdots + a_1y' + a_0y = 0$$ substitute $y = e^{rt}$ to obtain the characteristic equation: $$a_nr^n + a_{n-1}r^{n-1} + \cdots + a_1r + a_0 = 0.$$
Case 1 — Distinct Real Root $r$: Contributes $e^{rt}$ to general solution.

Case 2 — Repeated Real Root $r$ with multiplicity $m$: Contributes $$e^{rt},\; te^{rt},\; t^2e^{rt},\; \ldots,\; t^{m-1}e^{rt}.$$ These $m$ solutions are linearly independent.

Case 3 — Complex Conjugate Pair $\alpha \pm i\beta$ with multiplicity $m$: Contributes $2m$ real solutions: $$e^{\alpha t}\cos\beta t,\; e^{\alpha t}\sin\beta t,\; te^{\alpha t}\cos\beta t,\; te^{\alpha t}\sin\beta t,\; \ldots,\; t^{m-1}e^{\alpha t}\cos\beta t,\; t^{m-1}e^{\alpha t}\sin\beta t.$$
Example ($n=4$): $y^{(4)} - y = 0$. Characteristic: $r^4 - 1 = 0$ gives $r = \pm 1, \pm i$. General solution: $$y = c_1e^t + c_2e^{-t} + c_3\cos t + c_4\sin t.$$
Thm 9.1
17. Existence & Uniqueness for Systems
Theorem (Thm 9.1): Consider the first-order system IVP: $$\mathbf{x}' = A(t)\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{g}(t),\quad \mathbf{x}(t_0) = \mathbf{x}_0$$ where $\mathbf{x}$ is an $n$-component vector-valued function.

If all entries of $A(t)$ and $\mathbf{g}(t)$ are continuous on an open interval $I$ containing $t_0$, then there exists a unique solution $\mathbf{x}(t)$ defined on the entire interval $I$.

Proof idea: This is the vector version of Theorem 8.1. Rewrite as $\mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{f}(t, \mathbf{x})$ where $\mathbf{f}(t, \mathbf{x}) = A(t)\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{g}(t)$. Since $A(t)$ has continuous entries, $\mathbf{f}$ is continuous and Lipschitz in $\mathbf{x}$ (with Lipschitz constant $L = \max_t \|A(t)\|$). Picard iteration applies, yielding global existence on $I$.

For nonlinear systems: $\mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{f}(t, \mathbf{x})$ with $\mathbf{f}$ and $\partial\mathbf{f}/\partial\mathbf{x}$ continuous guarantees local existence and uniqueness (Picard–Lindelöf for systems).
Thm 9.2
18. Superposition for Homogeneous Systems
Theorem (Thm 9.2 — Superposition for Systems): If $\mathbf{x}^{(1)}, \mathbf{x}^{(2)}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}^{(n)}$ are solutions of the homogeneous linear system $$\mathbf{x}' = A(t)\mathbf{x},$$ then any linear combination $$\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1\mathbf{x}^{(1)}(t) + c_2\mathbf{x}^{(2)}(t) + \cdots + c_n\mathbf{x}^{(n)}(t)$$ is also a solution.

Proof: By linearity of matrix multiplication: $$\mathbf{x}' = c_1\mathbf{x}^{(1)'} + \cdots + c_n\mathbf{x}^{(n)'} = c_1A\mathbf{x}^{(1)} + \cdots + c_nA\mathbf{x}^{(n)} = A(c_1\mathbf{x}^{(1)} + \cdots + c_n\mathbf{x}^{(n)}) = A\mathbf{x}. \quad\blacksquare$$
Fundamental Matrix: If $\{\mathbf{x}^{(1)}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}^{(n)}\}$ are linearly independent, form the fundamental matrix $$\Psi(t) = [\mathbf{x}^{(1)}(t)\; \mathbf{x}^{(2)}(t)\; \cdots\; \mathbf{x}^{(n)}(t)].$$ Then $\Psi'(t) = A(t)\Psi(t)$, and the general solution is $\mathbf{x}(t) = \Psi(t)\mathbf{c}$ where $\mathbf{c} = (c_1, \ldots, c_n)^T$.
Thm 9.3
19. Liouville's Formula (Wronskian for Systems)
Theorem (Thm 9.3 — Liouville's Formula): Let $\mathbf{x}^{(1)}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}^{(n)}$ be solutions of $\mathbf{x}' = A(t)\mathbf{x}$ on interval $I$. Their Wronskian (as columns of $\Psi(t)$) satisfies $$W(t) = W(t_0) \exp\!\left(\int_{t_0}^t \text{tr}(A(s))\,ds\right)$$ where $\text{tr}(A) = a_{11} + a_{22} + \cdots + a_{nn}$ is the trace of $A$.

Proof sketch: For the Wronskian determinant $W(t) = \det\Psi(t)$, use Jacobi's formula: $$\frac{d}{dt}\det\Psi = (\det\Psi) \cdot \text{tr}(\Psi^{-1}\Psi').$$ Since $\Psi' = A\Psi$, we have $\Psi^{-1}\Psi' = \Psi^{-1}A\Psi$, and $\text{tr}(\Psi^{-1}A\Psi) = \text{tr}(A)$. Thus $W' = \text{tr}(A) \cdot W$, giving the result.

Note: Unlike the scalar case where $W$ decays as $\exp(-\int p_{n-1})$, for systems $W$ grows/decays as $\exp(\int \text{tr}(A))$. The sign depends on whether $\text{tr}(A) > 0$ or $< 0$.

Corollary: $W(t) \neq 0$ for all $t \in I$ if and only if $W(t_0) \neq 0$ for some $t_0 \in I$.
Method
20. Eigenvalue Method for Systems
Method (Constant Coefficients): For $\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$ with constant $n \times n$ matrix $A$, try $\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{rt}\mathbf{v}$.

Substituting: $re^{rt}\mathbf{v} = Ae^{rt}\mathbf{v}$, giving the eigenvalue problem: $$A\mathbf{v} = r\mathbf{v}.$$ Find eigenvalues from $\det(A - rI) = 0$, then eigenvectors from $(A - rI)\mathbf{v} = 0$.

Case 1 — Real Distinct Eigenvalues $r_1, \ldots, r_n$: With eigenvectors $\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_n$: $$\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1e^{r_1t}\mathbf{v}_1 + \cdots + c_n e^{r_nt}\mathbf{v}_n.$$
Case 2 — Complex $\lambda \pm i\mu$: If $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{a} + i\mathbf{b}$ is eigenvector for $\lambda + i\mu$: $$\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{\lambda t}[c_1(\mathbf{a}\cos\mu t - \mathbf{b}\sin\mu t) + c_2(\mathbf{a}\sin\mu t + \mathbf{b}\cos\mu t)].$$
Case 3 — Repeated Eigenvalues (Defective): If geometric multiplicity $<$ algebraic multiplicity, use generalized eigenvectors or matrix exponential (see Thm 11.1).
Thm 11.1
21. Matrix Exponential Properties
Definition: For an $n \times n$ matrix $A$, define $$e^{At} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{A^k t^k}{k!} = I + At + \frac{A^2t^2}{2!} + \frac{A^3t^3}{3!} + \cdots$$
Theorem (Properties):
  1. $e^{A \cdot 0} = I$ (identity)
  2. $\frac{d}{dt}e^{At} = Ae^{At} = e^{At}A$ (derivative)
  3. If $AB = BA$, then $e^{(A+B)t} = e^{At}e^{Bt} = e^{Bt}e^{At}$
  4. $e^{At}$ is invertible for all $t$, with $(e^{At})^{-1} = e^{-At}$
  5. For any invertible $P$: $e^{P^{-1}APt} = P^{-1}e^{At}P$ (similarity)

Solution to IVP: The unique solution to $\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$, $\mathbf{x}(0) = \mathbf{x}_0$ is $$\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At}\mathbf{x}_0.$$
For non-homogeneous: $\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{g}(t)$ has solution $$\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At}\mathbf{x}_0 + \int_0^t e^{A(t-s)}\mathbf{g}(s)\,ds.$$
Method
22. Computing Matrix Exponential
Method 1 — Diagonalization (if $A$ diagonalizable):
If $A = PDP^{-1}$ with $D = \text{diag}(r_1, \ldots, r_n)$: $$e^{At} = P e^{Dt} P^{-1} = P \cdot \text{diag}(e^{r_1t}, \ldots, e^{r_nt}) \cdot P^{-1}.$$
Method 2 — S-N Decomposition (for defective matrices):
Write $A = S + N$ where $S$ is diagonalizable, $N$ is nilpotent ($N^m = 0$ for some $m$), and $SN = NS$.
Then: $e^{At} = e^{St}e^{Nt} = e^{St}\left(I + Nt + \frac{N^2t^2}{2!} + \cdots + \frac{N^{m-1}t^{m-1}}{(m-1)!}\right).$
The series for $e^{Nt}$ terminates because $N^m = 0$.

Method 3 — Laplace Transform: $$e^{At} = \mathcal{L}^{-1}\{(sI - A)^{-1}\}.$$
Example (defective): $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. Here $S = I$, $N = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ with $N^2 = 0$. $$e^{At} = e^t \cdot (I + Nt) = e^t \begin{pmatrix} 1 & t \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}.$$
Method
23. Variation of Parameters (Systems)
Method: For non-homogeneous system $\mathbf{x}' = A(t)\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{g}(t)$, given a fundamental matrix $\Psi(t)$ for the homogeneous system.

Seek particular solution of form $\mathbf{x}_p(t) = \Psi(t)\mathbf{u}(t)$.

Substituting: $\Psi'\mathbf{u} + \Psi\mathbf{u}' = A\Psi\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{g}$. Since $\Psi' = A\Psi$, this reduces to $\Psi\mathbf{u}' = \mathbf{g}$.

Solution: $\mathbf{u}' = \Psi^{-1}\mathbf{g}$, so $$\mathbf{x}_p(t) = \Psi(t) \int \Psi^{-1}(t)\mathbf{g}(t)\,dt.$$
General solution: $\mathbf{x}(t) = \Psi(t)\mathbf{c} + \mathbf{x}_p(t)$.

For constant $A$: Take $\Psi(t) = e^{At}$, giving $$\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At}\mathbf{x}_0 + \int_{t_0}^t e^{A(t-s)}\mathbf{g}(s)\,ds.$$
This is the vector version of the variation of parameters formula, using the matrix exponential as the integrating factor.
